notes.text: For more than 8, poach the eggs in three or four batches, and keep the finished ones in a bowl of warm water while you cook the rest.

callback.body: In cacio e pepe, starchy water held melted cheese fat in a creamy sauce: an emulsion. Hollandaise is another emulsion. This time egg yolk does the holding, and melted butter is the fat.

move.title: Two gentle egg moves
move.body: Today you'll poach eggs, cooking them in water that's barely bubbling so the whites set soft around the yolk. And you'll make hollandaise, a warm, lemony butter sauce held together by egg yolks. They go on toasted English muffins with turkey bacon.

why.title: Egg yolk holds the butter
why.body: Egg yolk has a natural helper in it called lecithin. One end of it grabs water and the other grabs fat, so it wraps around tiny drops of butter and keeps them from joining up into a greasy puddle. That's what makes hollandaise thick and smooth.

why.title: Butter goes in slowly
why.body: The yolks can only wrap so many butter drops at a time. Pour the butter in a thin stream while you whisk, and each drop gets wrapped. Pour too fast and the sauce can't keep up, so it turns thin and oily. That's called breaking.

why.title: Barely bubbling water
why.body: Hard boiling water tosses an egg around and tears the white into stringy shreds. Water with just a few small bubbles lets the white settle and set in one soft piece around the yolk.

why.title: A splash of vinegar
why.body: A little vinegar in the water helps the egg white set faster, so it holds together instead of spreading out. You won't taste it.

why.title: Gentle heat for the yolks
why.body: The yolks cook over a pan of simmering water, not right on the burner. The steam warms them slowly, so they thicken without turning into scrambled eggs. Pasteurized eggs are used because the sauce is only lightly cooked.

wrong.sign: The hollandaise turned thin and oily
wrong.fix: Put a spoonful of hot water in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it a little at a time. It usually comes back together.

wrong.sign: The yolks look grainy, like tiny scrambled eggs
wrong.fix: They got too hot. Take the bowl off the pan right away and whisk hard. Next time, keep the water at a gentle simmer and lift the bowl off now and then.

wrong.sign: The poached egg whites are stringy
wrong.fix: The water was bubbling too hard. Turn it down so only a few small bubbles rise, and slide the next eggs in gently from a cup.
Whisk in a teaspoon of warm water at a time until it pours slowly from a spoon.

quiz.q: Why does the melted butter go into the yolks slowly?
choices: So the yolks can wrap each drop and the sauce doesn't break
quiz.explain: The yolk can only hold so much butter at once. Slow pouring keeps the sauce smooth.

quiz.q: What should the poaching water look like?
choices: Barely bubbling, just a few small bubbles
quiz.explain: Gentle water lets the white set softly in one piece.

substitutions.note: Lay a folded slice of smoked salmon on each muffin half instead. It doesn't need cooking.
Toast one slice of gluten-free bread for each egg.

steps.text: Cut the lemon in half. Squeeze the juice into the small bowl, using the fork to twist out the last of it. Pick out any seeds.
Put the butter for the hollandaise in the liquid measuring cup, cover it with a paper towel, and microwave it in short bursts until it's melted and hot.
steps.tip: Melted butter pops and spits in the microwave. Use 20-second bursts and stir between them.

steps.text: Pour about 2 inches of water into the saucepan and bring it to a gentle simmer over medium heat. Check that the bowl sits on top without touching the water.

Separate the {n:egg-pasteurized} pasteurized eggs: crack each one over the heatproof bowl and pass the yolk back and forth between the two half shells, letting the white drip into a cup below. Drop just the yolks into the bowl.
steps.tip: Save the whites in a covered container in the fridge. They make a good omelet or scramble tomorrow.

steps.text: Wash your hands with soap, and wipe the counter where the eggs were.
steps.tip: Raw egg can carry germs, even pasteurized ones. Clean hands before you touch anything else.

steps.text: Whisk the lemon juice and 1 tablespoon of water into the yolks. Set the bowl on the pan of simmering water and whisk without stopping until the yolks are pale, thick, and about twice as big.
steps.look: Pale yellow, thick, and the whisk leaves trails you can see for a second.
steps.tip: Hold the bowl with an oven mitt. If the edges start to look lumpy, lift the bowl off the pan for a few seconds and keep whisking.

steps.text: Slide the thermometer into the thickened yolks. They should read at least 160°F. If they don't, whisk over the water 30 seconds more and check again.

Turn off the heat, but leave the bowl on the pan. Whisking all the time, pour in the hot melted butter in a very thin stream, a little at a time. Whisk in the salt. Leave the bowl on the warm pan with the heat off until you need it.
steps.look: Thick, smooth, and glossy, like soft pudding. No oil on top.
steps.tip: If it starts looking oily, stop pouring and whisk hard until it's smooth again before adding more.

steps.text: Lay the turkey bacon in the skillet in one layer and cook over medium heat, turning it with the tongs, until it's browned and a little crisp. Move it to a plate lined with a paper towel. Cook the rest the same way.
Fill the large pot with about 3 inches of water, add the vinegar, and bring it to a boil. Then turn it down until just a few small bubbles rise.
Crack 4 of the regular eggs, each into its own cup or small bowl.
steps.tip: If you don't have 4 cups, crack them one at a time into the small bowl just before each goes in the water.

steps.text: Hold each cup right at the surface of the water and gently tip the egg in. Cook until the whites are completely set.
steps.look: The whites are firm and white all over, with no clear parts. The yolk jiggles a little.

steps.text: While the eggs poach, toast the English muffin halves in the toaster.

Lift one egg out with the slotted spoon and slide the thermometer sideways into the thick part of the white. It needs to read at least 160°F. If it doesn't, slip it back in for 1 more minute and check again.

Lift the eggs out with the slotted spoon, let them drain for a second, and set them on a paper towel. Poach the rest of the eggs the same way, 4 at a time, checking one from each batch. Wash your hands after each round of cracking.

Turn off the stove. On each plate, set 2 muffin halves, cut side up. Top each with a slice of turkey bacon, a poached egg, and a big spoonful of hollandaise. Sprinkle chives on top if you're using them.
steps.tip: Stir the hollandaise before you spoon it. If it has thickened, whisk in a teaspoon of warm water.
